_comment: Shahnama of Firdausi, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VI: Dara and Sikandar cycle. Paraphrase passages with notes.

title.en: Dara Stabbed by His Own Ministers

region.zh: 逃往克爾曼途中（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VI, Dara sec. 8

summary.en: Dara marches a third time against Sikandar with an army no longer bent on strife but broken-hearted and grown sick of war; the Iranians closed not with the Rumans hand to hand: they were the fox, the Rumans were the lion, and all the chiefs asked quarter. Dara turns away and flees lamenting with three hundred cavaliers and two ministers of high degree, Mahiyar and Janusiyar. Seeing the star so lofty thus set, they hold talk: Sikandar will give to us a province — and night gloomed, a storm arose, Janusiyar laid hand upon a dagger, stabbed the king upon the breast, that famed head reached its fall, and the troops deserted, one and all.
summary.zh: 大流士三度迎戰亞歷山大，然伊朗軍心已散——「他們是狐，羅馬人是獅」——眾將求饒。王泣而退走，身邊僅三百騎與兩位重臣馬希亞爾與賈努西亞爾。二人見王星已落，密議：「亞歷山大必封我等為省督！」夜黑風起，賈努西亞爾拔匕首刺入王胸，名王頭顱就此墜落，部眾作鳥獸散。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Alexander's Persianised biography (Sikandar). No living community restriction.

passages.text: When Dara led forth his troops, no army bent on strife, but broken-hearted and grown sick of war, the fortune of the Iranians drooped its head. They closed not with the Rumans hand to hand; they were the fox, the Rumans were the lion, and all the chiefs asked quarter, having come down from their pride to deep humility. Dara saw, turned away, and fled lamenting. With him there went three hundred cavaliers, the noblest of Iran.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Dara sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He had withal two ministers of high degree, who used to comrade him in fight. The name of one, an archimage, was Mahiyar, the other was called Janusiyar. These twain, on seeing their efforts fruitless and the star erewhile so lofty, and the glory of Dara thus set, held talk and said: this luckless man henceforth will see not crown and throne again; we needs must poniard him upon the breast, or smite his head with Indian sword. Sikandar will give to us a province. We shall be a crown upon the kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Dara sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Both of them, one minister, the other treasurer, went with the Shah; Janusiyar, the chief, upon the left hand, Mahiyar to right. Night gloomed, a storm arose, Janusiyar laid hand upon a dagger, stabbed the king upon the breast, that famed head reached its fall, and then the troops deserted, one and all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Dara sec. 8 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

region.zh: 大流士隕落之地（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VI, Dara sec. 9

summary.en: The ministers come to Sikandar saying they have slain his enemy, and the Ruman's heart and soul are filled with rage and grief: on drawing nigh he gazed upon Dara and saw his breast all blood. He takes on his lap the wounded monarch's head, removes the royal crown, unclasps the warrior's mail, and says: I will resign to thee the realm and throne; but these that thus have wronged thee will I hang head-downward from two gibbets presently. Dara, on hearing this, began to speak: death is much nearer to me than the throne; beware of saying I by mine own might prevailed o'er this famed people; know that good and ill are both of God, and while thou livest give Him the praise.
summary.zh: 二臣來報「已誅敵王」；亞歷山大聞言悲憤交加，趨近見大流士胸前皆血。他將垂死之王攬於膝上，摘其冠、解其甲，泣曰：「我願讓還江山王座；至於這二賊，我必倒懸其身於絞架！」大流士留言：「死比王座更近；切勿自誇『憑己力勝此名族』——善惡皆出於神，生時當頌揚祂。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: The ministers came to Sikandar, saying: O Shah victorious and endowed with knowledge! we have surprised and slain thine enemy; the crown and throne of chiefs are his no more. Sikandar, having heard Janusiyar, said thus to Mahiyar: where is the foe whom thou hast overthrown? Show me the way. The two led on. The Ruman's heart and soul were filled with rage and grief. On drawing nigh he gazed upon Dara and saw his breast all blood, his countenance like fenugreek.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Dara sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He gave orders to alight and set a guard o'er those two ministers, and then, dismounting as swift as wind himself, took on his lap the wounded monarch's head, and, tarrying until the stricken should begin to speak, chafed with his hands the visage of Dara, removing from the head the royal crown, unclasping from the breast the warrior's mail, while showering tears on him because no leech was then at hand: I will resign to thee the realm and throne; but these that thus have wronged thee will I hang head-downward from two gibbets presently.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Dara sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Dara, on hearing this, began to speak, and said: may wisdom alway be thy mate. Sure am I that thou wilt be recompensed by God, the all-holy Judge, for these thy words; but as for what thou saidst — Iran is thine — death is much nearer to me than the throne; high heaven so willeth, whose joy is travail and whose profit loss. Beware of saying: I by mine own might prevailed o'er this famed people. Know that good and ill are both of God, and while thou livest give Him the praise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Dara sec. 9 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Sikandar in the Gloom: Israfil and the Stones
title.zh: 亞歷山大入幽暗：伊斯拉菲爾與寶石之訓

region.en: The Gloom beyond the western dark (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 極西幽暗之地（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VI, Sikandar sec. 29

summary.en: Sikandar goes unattended toward the Fount of Life and prays: He will not die who nurtureth thus his soul; he takes two signets that shine like suns on water, one for his guide Khisr, who slips away to the Fount of Life, bathes, drinks, and returns apace. Sikandar finds a mountain with four aloewood columns, on each a huge green bird speaking in the Ruman tongue, and at the top beholds Israfil, with trump in hand and head uplifted, standing at his post, wind on his lips and moisture in his eye, till God shall bid him blow: O thou slave of greed! toil not so much, because some day a Call will reach thine ears. Then in the Gloom a voice cries: he that shall take a stone up from the road will grieve for what he beareth; and if he taketh none he will repent — and, emerging from the Gloom, each perceived the trick: their pockets were full of jewels.
summary.zh: 亞歷山大隻身尋訪「生命之泉」，攜兩枚遇水如日之印：一枚交引路人希茲爾——他卻悄然尋得聖泉、沐浴暢飲而歸。亞歷山大見山巔四根沉香柱、棲四隻操羅馬語的巨鳥；峰頂佇立著天使伊斯拉菲爾——號在唇邊、目含淚水，靜待神命：貪婪的僕人啊！莫要過勞，因為末日之號總會吹響。幽暗中又有聲音告誡：拾石者悔、不拾者亦悔——出得幽暗，才知囊中皆是寶石。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Gihon/Water-of-Life quest fused with the angel of the Trumpet. No living community restriction.

passages.text: He tarried there until the sun, grown pale, sank in that fount of lapis-lazuli; he saw the wonder wrought by holy God, the Bright One's disappearance from the world. He chose the most enduring of his troops, took with him food for forty days and more, and sought and found a guide. Khisr, who was chief among the nobles of that folk, advised him, and Sikandar said: if we shall obtain the Water of Life then we will pass much time in prayer. He will not die who nurtureth thus his soul, and in his wisdom refugeth with God. I have two signets that in sight of water shine out at night like suns. Take one, lead on; the other one shall light me on my way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 29 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Khisr left that station and all food behind him, and fared thus for two days and nights while none bestirred his lips to eat. Upon the third two ways showed mid the Darkness, and the Shah lost trace of Khisr. What while the prophet went toward the Fount of Life, exalting thus his living head to Saturn, bathed his body and head in that bright Water, sought no guard save God, drank, rested, and returned apace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 29 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sikandar reached the light and saw a mountain both high and bright, and on its top four columns of aloe-wood uplifted to the clouds; on every column was a mighty nest, and in each nest there sat a huge, green bird, which, speaking loudly in the Ruman tongue, hailed the victorious master of the world. He then descended and there saw Israfil, with trump in hand and head uplifted, standing at his post, wind on his lips and moisture in his eye, till God shall bid him blow. On seeing Sikandar he roared like thunder: O thou slave of greed! toil not so much, because some day a Call will reach thine ears.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 29 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: A cry ascended from the darksome heights: he that shall take a stone up from the road will grieve for what he beareth in his hand, and if he taketh none he will repent. The soldiers all gave ear; one man took of the stones; another left them; a third through indolence took little ones. When they reached the plain, emerging from the Gloom, each sought the truth and then perceived the trick: one had his bosom full of jewels cut, another his with jewels in the rough, and both regretted that they had so few; but sorrier still was he that picked up none.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 29 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Sikandar Bars Yajuj and Majuj Behind Iron and Naphtha
title.zh: 亞歷山大築鐵障禦雅朱者與馬朱者

region.en: Cloud-capt mountain range of the east (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 東方插雲山脈（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VI, Sikandar sec. 30

summary.en: Marching eastward Sikandar finds a noble city whose people bewail their fortune: by reason of this cloud-capt mountain-range our hearts are full of anguish, for Yajuj there and Majuj give us no sleep; their faces all resemble those of beasts, their tongues are black, their eyes like blood. The Shah builds the Barrier: the iron and molten naphtha poured between the mountain-walls shut the wild tribes out of the world, and God keepeth it till the Day of Doom, when the hosts of Yajuj and Majuj shall break forth upon the earth.
summary.zh: 亞歷山大東行至一富城，百姓泣訴：因這座插雲山脈，雅朱者與馬朱者使我們不得安眠——他們面如獸、舌黑、目如血。王乃於兩山之間築起鐵障，灌以熔化的石腦油，將野族封於世界之外；神守護此障至審判之日，屆時雅朱者與馬朱者的大軍將破障而出。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Gog-Magog wall shared with Qur'anic and Syriac traditions. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Two weeks he tarried and, when rested, marched. He set forth eastward, having seen the west; his purpose in the world was wayfaring. Now as he went he saw a noble city: no wind or dust passed o'er it, thou wouldst say. Whenas the drums beat on the elephants the chiefs came out two miles to welcome him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 30 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: They loosed their tongues and thus bewailed their fortune: a very grievous case confronteth us, and we will tell it to the conquering Shah. By reason of this cloud-capt mountain-range our hearts are full of anguish, toil, and grief. Since for resistance we are powerless Yajuj there and Majuj give us no sleep, for when a portion of them reach our city our portion is all misery and travail. Their faces all resemble those of beasts, their tongues are black, their eyes like blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 30 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Shah bade smelt the iron and pour the molten naphtha between the mountain-walls, and built the Barrier which God keepeth till the Day of Doom, when the hosts of Yajuj and Majuj shall break forth upon the earth. So he made the world secure behind iron, and marched on, leaving the tribes to rage beyond the wall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 30 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Speaking Tree Foretells Sikandar's Death

region.en: Grove of the twin tree (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雙幹神樹林（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VI, Sikandar sec. 31

summary.en: Sikandar comes to a tree with two trunks and birds that speak. When Sol attained the apex of heaven's vault Sikandar heard aloft a cry proceeding from the leaves: why doth Sikandar roam so o'er the world, for he hath had his portion of good things, and, when he shall have reigned for twice seven years, must quit the throne of sovereignty? The female branches say: thou hast not long to live; do not thyself cloud and contract thy days. And the speaking tree said to the Shah: be speedy, and bind the baggage on; thy mother, kindred in Rum, and face-veiled ladies there will look on thee no more. Death in an alien land will come ere long.
summary.zh: 亞歷山大行至一株雙幹神樹，樹上有會說話的飛鳥。日中時分，樹葉間傳出可怕的預言：「亞歷山大啊，你已得世間應得之分；十四年之後必須讓出王座！」另一側的枝葉更道：「你命不久長，莫再自苦短日。」神樹直告：「速速收拾行裝；羅馬的母親與眷屬再也見不到你——客死異鄉之日不遠了。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the oracular trees of the sun and moon. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When Sol attained the apex of heaven's vault Sikandar heard aloft a cry proceeding from the leaves of that tall tree, an awful, boding cry. He feared and asked of the interpreter: shrewd, trusty friend! what say the talking leaves, because they bathe my heart in lymph of blood? The guide replied: the leaves upon the boughs of this tree say: why doth Sikandar roam so o'er the world, for he hath had his portion of good things, and, when he shall have reigned for twice seven years, must quit the throne of sovereignty?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 31 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sikandar wept tears of blood; the guide's words wrung his heart. Thenceforth he spake to no one, but remained all sorrowful till midnight. Then the leaves upon the other trunk gave utterance. What is it that the other branches say? asked the Shah, and his informant solved the mystery: the female branches say: thou travailest in this wide world for greed and for addition. Thou hast not long to live; do not thyself cloud and contract thy days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 31 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The great king asked of the interpreter: inquire if I shall be in Rum when my dark day shall come, and if my mother see me not alive will she at last enshroud this face of mine? The speaking tree said to the Shah: be speedy, and bind the baggage on. Thy mother, kindred in Rum, and face-veiled ladies there will look on thee no more. Death in an alien land will come ere long; crown, diadem, and throne grow tired of thee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 31 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Coffin of Sikandar and the Sages' Lament
title.zh: 亞歷山大之柩與智者輓歌

region.zh: 亞歷山大里亞城（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VI, Sikandar secs. 37-39

summary.en: Knowing that his time was near, Sikandar bids carry his throne to the field; with failing voice he says: be devout, wise, modest, and heed all my last requests — and his life departed. They fired his palace, docked a thousand steeds, bore the golden bier out to the plain, and laved the corpse with rose-water and camphor; the wise Arastalis laid his hand on that strait coffin, saying: God-fearing Shah! where are thy prudence, knowledge, and rede that this strait coffin should become thy home? Another said: soon shall we be as thou art, thou that wast an uncut gem; another: why in this Wayside Inn laboriously didst thou employ thyself, since a narrow coffin is thine only wealth?
summary.zh: 自知大限將至，亞歷山大命人將御座抬至戰場，以微弱之聲囑託後事，隨即駕崩。全軍縞素、焚其宮殿、千馬斷鞍；金輦抬出，聖水香樟浴其遺體。賢者亞里士多德按柩而問：「敬神的王啊，你的智謀與遠見何在，竟讓這狹小棺槨成了你的居所？」群賢輓唱：「我們不久也將如此——你原是未雕之璞玉」；「你在這驛館中苦苦經營，所換得的唯有這口窄棺！」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: And knowing that his time was near, Sikandar bade carry from the palace to the field his throne. The troops bewailed his malady when they beheld the Shah's pale face. With failing voice said Caesar: be devout, wise, modest, and heed all my last requests, if ye would prosper both in soul and body. When I have gone the work is left for you, and fortune is not dealing ill with me. He spake, his life departed, and that Shah so famous, that host-shatterer, passed away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 37 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: A cry went up from all the host and split the ears of heaven. The soldiers all strewed dust upon their heads. They fired his palace, and docked a thousand steeds, reversing all their saddles. They bore the golden bier out to the plain; a prelate laved the corpse with clear rose-water, and besprinkled thereon pure camphor. Of gold-woven brocade they made his winding-sheet, and, having shrouded thus that noble form beneath brocade of Chin, they covered it with honey to the feet and then sealed down the lid of that strait coffin: passed away that Tree so fruitful and so shadowing!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar sec. 37 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: They set his coffin on the plain; all earth was full of hue and cry, and above a hundred thousand flocked to Iskandariya to the coffin. The wise Arastalis stood forth and laid his hand on that strait coffin, saying: God-fearing Shah! where are thy prudence, knowledge, and rede that this strait coffin should become thy home? Another said: soon shall we be as thou art, thou that wast an uncut gem. Another said: why in this Wayside Inn laboriously didst thou employ thyself, since this is all that thou hast gained by toil? A narrow coffin is thine only wealth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Sikandar secs. 38-39 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
